extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, historians, and policymakers interested in colonial policy and fiscal theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical political-economy criteria for evaluating monopolies, colonial dominion, and taxation (Adam Smith-style analysis). Focuses on when a province is advantageous to an empire, effects of mercantile monopoly, and practical schemes for colonial taxation and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly's net effect on national revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly raises the rate of mercantile profit and thereby augments somewhat the gain of our merchants, but it obstructs the natural increase of capital and tends rather to diminish than to increase the sum total of the revenue which the inhabitants of the country derive from the profits of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mechanism: monopoly raises mercantile profit (benefiting a narrow order) but discourages improvement of land and accumulation of capital, keeps market interest higher, reduces abundance of wages, rent, and profits overall. Concludes the single advantage to one order is frequently hurtful to the general interest of the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of profit rates on capital allocation and land improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the profit from mercantile employment is greater than that from the application of capital to land improvement, capital will be drawn from mercantile employments to land, and vice versa; whatever raises the rate of mercantile profit either lessens the superiority or increases the inferiority of profit from improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate how policy (e.g., monopoly) shifts capital away from productive land-improvement, thereby retarding natural increases in rent and land prices (land price in proportion to rent falls as interest rises).

rubrics_metrics.name: High mercantile profits reduce accumulation (behavioral criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The high rate of profit seems everywhere to destroy that parsimony which, in other circumstances, is natural to the character of the merchant; accumulation is thus prevented in the hands of all those who are naturally the most disposed to accumulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues as an evaluative rule that policies producing persistently high merchant profits encourage luxury and dissipate funds that would otherwise be saved and invested productively, diminishing productive capital over time (example comparisons: Cadiz and Lisbon vs. Amsterdam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a province to be advantageous to the empire
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to render any province advantageous to the empire to which it belongs, it ought to afford, in time of peace, a revenue to the public, sufficient not only for defraying the whole expense of its own peace establishment, but for contributing its proportion to the support of the general government of the empire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a standard to judge colonial value: compare ordinary and extraordinary revenues (peace and wartime) to the costs the province imposes on the empire; if a province does not contribute its share, an unequal burden falls elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits of relying on colony assemblies for imperial taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The colony assemblies can never be so managed as to levy upon their constituents a public revenue sufficient to maintain their civil and military establishment and to pay their proper proportion of the expense of the general government of the British empire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: distance from sovereign, dispersed situation, various constitutions, and inability to distribute offices among leading members make assemblies hard to manage centrally; assemblies lack means and information to judge defence/support needs of the whole empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation-by-requisition as a conditional mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been proposed that the colonies should be taxed by requisition, the parliament of Great Britain determining the sum which each colony ought to pay, and the provincial assembly assessing and levying it in the way that suited best the circumstances of the province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment: this scheme centralizes determination of empire-wide burdens while leaving local assessment to colonies. It may be reasonable if parliamentary requisitions remain proportionate to what is paid at home, but it risks non-enforcement and evasion; parliament would need means to render requisitions immediately effectual in case of evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality / virtual representation principle for just taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contribution of the colonies was to rise or fall in proportion to the rise or fall of the land-tax, parliament could not tax them without taxing its own constituents, and the colonies might, in this case, be considered as virtually represented in parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to judge fairness of taxation: linking colonial contributions to a common tax base (e.g., land-tax) or proportional representation would make parliamentary taxation more legitimate and reduce objections that colonies are taxed without representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation as a remedy for colonial resistance to taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: If to each colony which should detach itself from the general confederacy, Great Britain should allow such a number of representatives as suited the proportion of what it contributed to the public revenue of the empire... a new method of acquiring importance... would be presented to the leading men of each colony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: offering proportionate representation in the imperial legislature would preserve the importance of colonial elites, provide an incentive to accept taxation, and reduce likelihood of violent resistance; union with representation is proposed as a solution to secure peace and mutual benefit.
